posts.title: Making Number Gacha
posts.subtitle: Does a gacha game still work without its sexy anime girls?
body: Last month I released Number Gacha, a game where you roll, unpack, and battle numbers. Thank you to everyone who’s played! In my inaugural blog post, I wanted to look back on the project that has consumed the last six months of my life and figure out why it’s struck such a chord.
What Makes a Game Fun?

Let’s take a step back and start with this question. Is it slowly mastering a skill, or a satisfying progression of power? Is it a well-written, emotional story? Is it the thrill of shooting that last annoying enemy in the face?

These things are all fun— of course they are. But lately, I’ve been drawn to a different kind of engagement, one that feels cheaper. Games that include virtual roulette wheels or shiny loot boxes, where each rare item I get triggers a dopamine hit in my brain. Why is something so crudely stimulating, such thinly veiled gambling, just as fun to me as a “real game”?

It feels akin to doomscrolling, trying to rack up as much stimulation as possible to keep my brain happy and sedated. Perversely, it actually started to make sense. I’m tired after a long day, or want to take a break, and need something fast and quick. Why work for my fun through difficult, rewarding gaming when it can be served to me by a single click?

So is my attention span shot? Probably. Should I be concerned about my compulsion for quick, brainless stimulation? Almost definitely. But instead of examining everything in a boring, academic way, why don’t we make a game out of it?
And thus Number Gacha was born.
Wait, Gacha?

I went with Gacha because it’s the genre with perhaps the most thinly veiled gambling out there. The example I like to use to explain gacha games is opening pack of Pokémon cards. Is there a ultra-rare holographic Blastoise in your pack? Probably not. But there could be, so you line up early at Costco to stock up and rip packs from the hands of children in your way. Now, add an obscured premium currency, dozens of microtransactions, and a new legendary character that comes out each month, and you get modern gacha games.

You might have noticed Number Gacha looks a bit different. There’s no monetization or cute anime girls (sorry). Instead of a convoluted currency system, a pull costs one diamond, which refreshes every minute. If you run out of diamonds, you can do math problems to get more.

All this is because, besides not having the production budget of a full-blown game studio, I wanted to test if just gacha mechanics are enough to get a player hooked. The thrill of a legendary pull! The satisfaction of ripping open a pack! Strip away all the fancy characters and gimmicks and world-building; can the player become just as invested in numbers?
Making the Game

Even though I wanted the game to feel “stripped back”, it still pained me to make it ugly. So I found a dither shader online that worked with React, and modified it to what I needed. The number backgrounds are probably the most obvious place it's showcased, but I added a touch of dithering everywhere to create a nice visual through line.

Packs in particular were a must for me from the beginning. Who doesn’t love opening a pack? I drew from inspirations such as TCG Pocket, which makes it feel amazing to drag your finger across a digital pack, and Balatro, with its zany, memorable pack art.

At this point I thought I was cooking, but while showing the game around I realized this might not be enough; people craved an activity with their numbers, something that showed them off. At the same time, there needed to be a more compelling reason to get duplicates of numbers and level them up. And so I implemented a combat system, which simultaneously felt like a ridiculous addition to a game about numbers and a no-brainer solution to my problems.

I took inspiration from A Dark Room’s simple, reflex-based combat, and added a mathematical twist. The numbers themselves act as both their health and attack. Factors of the enemy are extra effective against it. And then there’s division!
With all of these parts in place I felt like I had a real, compelling game.
So What's the Takeaway?
Kind of a rude question to ask, but okay. Let me turn the question back to you, player. You've played the game. Are you having fun?

If so, then I think I’ve succeeded. My brain might still be a slave to the algorithm, but at least I can think about why, about the complex balance of vices and rewards that drive all of us. Maybe I’ve even made you think about it, too.
